segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We spoke about how we have two verbs for to be in Spanish, estar and ser, and we practiced

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: with estar, which is the verb that we use for states.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we said that the word "state" is related to estar. Actually, it's it's like the same word. What looks most different

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: there between "state" and estar is that E that you get at the beginning of estar. But

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you will find this actually with words that start ST-, SP-, S and consonant.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You can't begin a word like this in Spanish where you can in English. So actually,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you will find many words between English and Spanish that get like an extra E at the beginning in Spanish. For example, the word "Spanish".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There you have the O splitting of "school" to UE, escuela.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you think you might say strict if it's the same word in English and Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estricto. Good. "spectacular", it's the same word as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is the difference that we see between "state" and estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we said that estar we use with what we will consider states

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now with what we consider characteristics of being, we will use ser,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and we said that ser all by itself means being.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un ser is a being. Un ser humano

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Here humano is acting like an adjective, so it's coming afterwards.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But it will also be a noun. We can say "the human".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El humano. And there it's a noun.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But el ser humano, there it's an adjective.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "I am" from ser is soy. Soy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So like estoy from estar, it ends -oy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There are just four verbs in the whole Spanish language that use -oy

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: from dar, to give. Doy, I'm giving. And then

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we said that "student" is estudiante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you wanted to say "I am a student"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "it is" or "she is", "he is", "you are" (to usted),

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we learned it already, but we didn't learn that it was from ser.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "it is possible"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es posible. Good, so we have es. Es is from ser. Now ser is more irregular

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: than estar. It doesn't look like es is from ser, not too much.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then we had "they are" or "you guys are". What was that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've got three of the versions now: soy,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can take son and we can work out the "we" form from son working backwards.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now we said that working backwards means taking off the consonant that you know associates to "they"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and putting on the ending that associates to "we", for example.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to go from son (they are) to "we are", how do you think it will sound?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which leaves one left, which is the "you" informal, which is eres.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Eres. So, let's make a recap.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Soy. And if you want to use the word for "I"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And if you want to use the word for "he"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Son. And what if you wanted to use the word for "they"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A nice way to remember "they" as well is you can make "she" plural and you will get the feminine "they".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ellos son, ellas son. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "you guys" is the plural of that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ustedes. So it's the plural of usted, but it's not necessarily

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Only in some parts of Spain, which we will talk about later, but everywhere else in the Spanish-speaking world this is just how you refer to "you guys".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It doesn't sound formal anymore when it becomes plural. So how would you say "you guys are"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ustedes son. Good. And then we have "we are"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Somos or nosotros somos. Or if we were an all-female group?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then we have the "you" informal, which is eres, which is probably the weirdest

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can relate it to es, maybe they are similar, es, eres.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "you are", using the word for "you"?

segments.text: So how would I say, using estar, "How is he?", "How is he doing?"

segments.text: if I want to ask you "What is he like?", maybe you tell me about your new boss

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: or a new friend, and I ask you

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "What is he like?" or "What is she like?", am I referring to their state
